newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek farmers let foreign trucks through blockade.
newsitem.headline: Greek farmers let foreign trucks through blockade.

text.p: Greek farmers let a few foreign truckers drive through their barricades on Thursday for the first time since they started blocking Greece's highways 15 days ago with thousands of tractors in a nationwide protest.

Farmers vowed to continue the blockade to press their demands for cheaper fuel and equipment, and state subsidies on products, especially cotton -- in a protest that has paralysed overland transport throughout the country.

"We opened the roadblocks for two hours as a gesture of good will to foreign truck drivers. But our struggle continues and as of tonight nothing will get through," said Thanassis Nasikas, a farmers' representative.

Some 700 foreign trucks have been stranded in Greece during the two-week blockade with drivers -- mostly British, Dutch, Bulgarian and Turkish -- complaining of a lack of food and water and poor sanitation.
The blockade, with thousands of tractors in some 100 key junctions, showed signs of easing with vehicles being pulled back from smaller roads in central and northern Greece.
Prime Minister Costas Simitis has maintained a wait-and-see policy saying he would not send police to open the roads but at the same time said could not satisfy the farmers' demands.
Export companies, hoteliers and industrialists put damages from the blockade so far at $500 million and said they were rising fast.
The borders with Turkey and Bulgaria have also been blocked and the Association of Northern Greek Exporters said exports in December had dropped by 42 percent.
Simitis fears that giving in to the farmers' demands would open a Pandora's box for other working groups, hard hit by next year's austerity budget, to take similar action.
"Demands for billions of drachmas cannot be satisfied. To do so would be a step backwards," Simitis said this week.
Teachers, state doctors, customs and taxation employees, port workers and diplomats are either striking or plan strikes until December 19, when parliament votes on the budget.
Several hundred construction workers marched through Athens to the parliament on Thursday, the latest in a string of unhappy workers groups to take to the streets.
Simitis, facing his first crisis since winning elections in September, left for Dublin's European Union summit on Wednesday with a skeleton staff of diplomats.
Most diplomats have been on strike since December 6 to protest against a new tax on an allowance given to diplomats abroad to cover living and travelling expenses.
The budget, aimed to set the course for Greece to join the European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 2001, cuts state hiring, abolishes most tax exemptions and imposes new levies.
The two biggest labour confederations have called a one-day nationwide strike for December 17 and many unions have declared a three-day stoppage at that time.
